extracted.intended_audience: astronomers / natural philosophers / readers of a scientific treatise (Latin)
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of labeled propositions, problems and theorems from a classical Latin treatise (astronomy/physics) giving methods, calculations, and explanations for planetary motion, Earth's figure, pendulum experiments, satellite motions and tides.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XV. PROBLEMA I. Invenire orbium principales diametros
rubrics_metrics.description: Capiendae sunt hse in ratione subsesquiplicata temporum periodorum, per prop. xv lib. i; deinde sigillatim augendae in ratione summae massarum solis & planetse cujusque revolventis ad primam duarum medie proportionaHum inter summam illam & solem, per prop. LX Hb. I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction: take these quantities in the sesqui‑plicate ratio of their orbital periods (per prop. xv lib. i); then augment individually in the ratio of the sum of the masses of the Sun and each revolving planet to the first of the two mean proportions between that sum and the Sun (per prop. LX lib. I). (This gives the principal diameters of the orbits.)

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XVI. PROBLEMA II. Invenire orbium eccentricitates & aphelia
rubrics_metrics.description: Problema confit per prop. xviii Hb. i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference: solution follows from the method given in proposition xviii of book I; no extended exposition here.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XVII. THEOREMA XV. Planetarum motus diferentes uniformes esse, & librationem lunae ex ipsius motu diurno oriri
rubrics_metrics.description: Patet per motus legem i, & corol. 22 prop. lxvi lib. i. Jupiter respectu fixarum revolvitur horis 9 56', mars horis 24 39', venus horis 23 circiter, terra horis 23 56', sol diebus 25 1 & luna diebus 27 hor. 7. 43'. Haec ita se habere ex phaenomenis manifestum est. Maculae in corpore solis ad eundem situm in disco solis redeunt diebus 27I circiter respectu terrae; ideoque respectu fixarum sol revolvitur diebus 25 circiter. Quoniam vero lunae circa axem suum uniformiter revolventis dies menstruus est: hujus facies eadem ulteriorem umbilicum orbis ejus semper respiciet quamproxime, & propterea pro situ umbilici illius deviabit hinc inde a terra. Haec est libratio lunae in longitudinem. Libratio in latitudinem orta est ex latitudine lunae & inclinatione axis ejus ad planum eclipticae. (Mentio analogorum motuum satellitum Saturni & Jovii.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: gives observed rotation/diurnal periods and uses them to deduce lunar libration in longitude and latitude; applies similar reasoning to Saturn's and Jupiter's satellites and notes observational evidence (spots on Sun and Jupiter) supporting these inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XVIII. THEOREMA XVI. Axes planetarum diametris quae ad eosdem axes normaliter ducti sunt minores esse
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetae sublato omni motu circulari diurno figuram sphaericam, ob aequalem undique partium gravitatem, affectare deberent. Per motum illum circularem fit ut partes ab axe recedentes juxta aequatorem ascendere conentur. Ideoque materia si fluida sit ascensu suo ad aequatorem diametros adaugebit, axem vero descensu suo ad polos diminuet. Sic jovis diameter brevior deprehenditur inter polos quam ab oriente in occidentem. Eodem argumento, nisi terra nostra paulo altior esset sub aequatore quam ad polos, maria ad polos subsiderent, & juxta aequatorem ascendendo ibi omnia inundarent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: rotation produces equatorial bulging and polar flattening. Observational consequence: Jupiter (and other rotating planets) should be oblate; consequences for terrestrial seas and Earth’s shape are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XIX. PROBLEMA III. Invenire proportionem axis planetae ad diametros eidem perpendiculares
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed measurements (Norwood, Picart, Cassinus) and calculations are used to derive Earth's circumference, semidiameter and the proportion of equatorial to polar diameters. From measured arcs and pendulum data the text computes semidiameter in Parisian feet and deduces equatorial vs polar diameter ratio leading to an equatorial excess (diameter ratio 230:229 and equatorial excess ≈ 85472 Parisian feet ≈ certain miles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long worked example: uses geodetic arcs, arc‑to‑foot conversions, free‑fall and centrifugal force computations, and combinations of ratios (126:125, 100:101 etc.) to deduce that gravities at equator vs pole and thus the flattening. Also applies same reasoning to Jupiter to estimate its oblateness; notes observational confirmation (Cassini, Poicendices, Poincets measurements) and mentions dependence on density and rotation rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XX. PROBLEMA IV. Invenire & iter se comparare pondera corporum in terrae hujus regionibus diversis
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows that weights of equal columns of fluid or bodies at different places are proportional to distances from Earth's center; deduces that increment of weight going from equator to poles is approximately proportional to the square of the sine of latitude (sin^2 latitude). Presents a table of pendulum lengths and arc measures for latitudes from 0° to 90° and concludes the inequality of degrees is small so Earth may be approximated by a sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives theoretical relation between weight and latitude (increment ∝ square of sine of latitude) and tabulates predicted pendulum length/degree length by latitude. Provides discussion of experimental pendulum observations (Richer, Halley, Varin & Des Hayes, Couplet, etc.) that pendula are shorter near equator, and analysis of observational errors, thermal effects on rods, and conclusion about Earth's equatorial bulge and possible internal density variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXI. THEOREMA XVII. Puncta aequinoctialia regredi, & axem terrae singulis revolutionibus annuis nutando bis inclinari in eclipticam & bis redire ad positionem priorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Patet per corol. 20 prop. lxvi lib. i. Motus tamen iste nutandi perexiguus esset debet, & vix aut ne vix quidem sensibilis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: the equinoctial points regress (precession) and Earth's axis nutates twice per year relative to the ecliptic, but the amplitude is extremely small (negligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXII. THEOREMA XVIII. Motus omnes lunares, omnesque motuum inaequalitates ex allatis principiis consequi
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas majores posse alios minores deferre etc.; actione solis perturbabuntur eorum motus multimode, iisque adficientur inaequalitatibus quae in luna nostra notantur. Haec (per corol. 2,3,4,5 prop. lxvi) velocius movetur, ac radio ad terram ducto describit aream pro tempore majorem, orbemque habet minus curvum atque ideo propius accedit ad terram in syzygiis quam in quadraturis, nisi quatenus impedit motus eccentricitatis. Eccentricitas maxima est ubi apogaeum lunae in syzygiis versatur & minima in quadraturis; luna in perigeo velocior & propior, in apogaeo tardior & remotior. Progreditur apogæum & regrediuntur nodi, sed motu inaequabili; apogaeum velocior progreditur in syzygiis suis, tardius regreditur in quadraturis, & excessus progressus supra regressum annuatim fertur in consequentia. Nodi quiescunt in syzygiis & velocissime regrediuntur in quadraturis. Sunt et alia inaequalitates a prioribus non observatae, quas motus lunares adeo perturbantur ut nulla lege certam reduci possint; varias quantities (velocitates apogaei & nodorum, differentia eccentricitatum, variatio) augentur & diminuuntur annuatim in triplicata ratione diametri apparentis solaris, & variatio etiam in duplica ratione temporis inter quadraturas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive statement of lunar inequalities derived from gravitational principles: describes eccentricity, apogee/perigee behavior, node motion, variation and other perturbations; notes annual modulation related to apparent solar diameter and complicated irregularities not yet reducible to simple law; mentions astronomical practice of subsuming some inequalities under lunar prosthaphaeresis in calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXIII. PROBLEMA V. Motus inequaleles satellitum jovis & saturni a motibus lunaribus derivare
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex motibus lunae nostrae motus analogi lunarum seu satellitum jovis sic derivantur. Motus medii nodorum satellitum extremi jovialis est ad motum medium nodorum lunae nostrae in ratione composita ex ratione dupHcata temporis periodici terrae circa solem ad tempus periodicum jovis circa solem & ratione simplici temporis periodici satellitis circa jovem ad tempus periodicum lunae circa terram (per corol. 16 prop. lxvi lib. i). Ideoque annis centum conficiunt nodus iste 8' 24' in antecedentia. Motus medii nodorum satellitum interiorum sunt ad motum hujus ut illorum tempora periodica ad tempus periodicum hujus. Motus autem augis satellitis cujusque in consequentia est ad motum nodorum ipsius in antecedentia ut motus apogaei lunae nostrae ad hujus motum nodorum. Diminui tamen debet motus augis inventus in ratione 5 ad 9 vel 1 ad 2 circiter ob causam quam hic exponere non vacat. Equations maximae nodorum & augis satellitis fere sunt ad aequationes maximas nodorum & augis lunae respective ut motus nodorum temporibus quibus satellites & luna ad solem revolvuntur, per idem corollarium; ideoque in satellite extimo non superat 5' 12'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives proportional relations between lunar perturbation quantities and analogous satellite (Jovian, Saturnian) quantities via ratios of periodic times; provides numerical example for nodal motion and bounds on variations; notes caveats (reduction factors ~5:9 or 1:2) without full derivation here.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPOSITIO XXIV. THEOREMA XIX. Fluxum & refluxum maris ab actionibus solis ac lunae oriri
rubrics_metrics.description: Mare singulis diebus tam lunaribus quam solaribus bis intumescere ac bis defluere debere ac bis defluere patet per corol. 19 & 20 prop. lxvi lib. i ut & aquae maximam altitudinem, in maribus profundis & liberis, appulsum luminarium ad meridianum loci minori quam sex horarum spatio sequi, uti fit in maris Atlantici & Ethiopici tractu toto orientali inter Galliam & promontorium Bonne Spei ut & in maris Pacifici littore Chilensi & Peruviano: in quibus littoribus aestus in horam circiter secundam tertiam vel quartam incidit, nisi ubi motus ab oceano profundo per loca vadosa propagatus usque ad horam quintam sextam septimam aut ultra retardatur. Horas numero ab appulsu luminariis utriusque ad meridianum loci, tam infra horizontem quam supra, & per horas diei lunaris intelligo vigesimas quartas partes temporis quo luna motu apparente diurno ad meridianum loci revertitur. Vis solis vel lunae ad mare elevandum maxima est in ipso appulsu luminarii ad meridianum loci. Sed vis eo tempore in mare impressa manet aliquandiu & per vim novam subinde impressam augetur, donec mare ad altitudinem maximam ascendit, id quod fiet spatio horae unius duarumve sed saepius ad spatio horarum trium circiter vel etiam plurium si mare sit vadosum. ... (continues with composition of solar & lunar effects at syzygies/quadratures, dependence on distances/perigee/perihelion, declination effects, decomposition into northern/southern tidal hemispheres, diagrams describing maxima timings at three hours after transit etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed tidal theory: tides arise from combined solar and lunar actions producing two daily rises and falls; timing of maxima roughly three hours after meridian transit of the relevant body, modulated by syzygies (spring tides), quadratures (neap tides), distances (perigee/apogee and perihelion/aphelion), declination from equator (latitude effects), and local propagation delays in shallow or confined waters. Includes geometric construction to predict where and when maxima/minima occur and distinguishes northern vs southern tidal hemispheres; gives observational examples (Atlantic, Pacific coasts) and expected timing delays in estuaries and river mouths.
